    DxPower

    The goal of DxPower is to provide functions for power and sample size calculation in confirmatory diagnostic accuracy trials.

    The methodology is based on asymptotic normal approximations and an intersection–union testing framework, where both co-primary endpoints (i.e.sensitivity and specificity) must reject their respective null hypotheses.

    Installation

    You can install the development version of DxPower from GitHub with:

    # install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("CTU-Bern/DxPower")

    Current Implementation Status

    The current version implements sample size determination and power evaluation for confirmatory diagnostic accuracy studies with:

    • Binary endpoints (sensitivity and specificity)

    • One-sided superiority hypotheses

    • Co-primary testing using an intersection–union framework

    • Wald-type asymptotic normal approximations

    Extensions to non-inferiority settings, continuous endpoints, and more general co-primary objectives are planned.

    Statistical Framework

    Study Setting

    We consider a confirmatory diagnostic accuracy study with:

    • Sensitivity SeSe
    • Specificity SpSp
    • Disease prevalence π\pi
    • Total sample size NN

    The number of diseased (cases) and non-diseased (control) subjects is:

    NSe=Nπ,NSp=N(1−π)N_{Se}=N\pi, N_{Sp}=N(1-\pi)

    Diseased and non-diseased subjects form disjoint subgroups. Under standard binomial sampling assumptions, the corresponding estimators of sensitivity and specificity are asymptotically independent.

    Hypotheses

    We consider one-sided superiority hypotheses:

    For sensitivity:

    H0,Se:Se≤Se0vsH1,Se:Se>Se0 H_{0,Se}: Se \le Se_0 \quad\text{vs}\quad H_{1,Se}: Se > Se_0

    For specificity:

    H0,Sp:Sp≤Sp0vsH1,Sp:Sp>Sp0 H_{0,Sp}: Sp \le Sp_0 \quad\text{vs}\quad H_{1,Sp}: Sp > Sp_0

    Each endpoint is tested at level α=0.025\alpha = 0.025.

    Because both null hypotheses must be rejected to declare overall success, an intersection–union test (IUT) framework is used. Under the global null hypothesis the overall Type I error rate is controlled at level α\alpha without multiplicity adjustment.

    Test Statistic and Approximation

    Both endpoints are evaluated using a Wald-type normal approximation. Under large-sample theory:

    Sê∼N(Se,Se(1−Se)NSe),Sp̂∼N(Sp,Sp(1−Sp)NSp)\hat{Se} \sim N\left( Se,\; \frac{Se(1-Se)}{N_{Se}} \right),\hat{Sp} \sim N\left( Sp,\; \frac{Sp(1-Sp)}{N_{Sp}} \right)

    The sample size formula uses the classical normal approximation with:

    • Variance under the null: Var(Se0)=Se0(1−Se0),Var(Sp0)=Sp0(1−Sp0)Var(Se_0)=Se_0(1-Se_0), Var(Sp_0)=Sp_0(1-Sp_0)
    • Variance under the alternative: Var(Se1)=Se1(1−Se1),Var(Sp1)=Sp1(1−Sp1)Var(Se_1)=Se_1(1-Se_1), Var(Sp_1)=Sp_1(1-Sp_1)

    Overall Power Definition

    Because both endpoints must reject the null hypothesis, an intersection–union test (IUT) is applied.

    Assuming asymptotic independence:

    PowerSe×PowerSp=Poweroverall Power_{Se} \times Power_{Sp}=Power_{overall}

    (1−βSe)×(1−βSp)=(1−βOverall) (1-\beta_{Se}) \times (1-\beta_{Sp})=(1-\beta_{Overall})

    Individual endpoint powers are therefore typically larger than the target overall power.

    Functions

    ss_opt_bin()

    Computes the required total sample size for a desired overall power and true prevalence π\pi in a confirmatory diagnostic accuracy study with co-primary endpoints.

    Sample Size Formula

    For sensitivity:

    NSe=(z1−αSe0(1−Se0)+z1−βSeSe1(1−Se1))2π×(Se1−Se0)2 N_{Se} = \frac{\left( z_{1-\alpha} \sqrt{Se_0(1-Se_0)} + z_{1-\beta_{Se}} \sqrt{Se_1(1-Se_1)} \right)^2} {\pi \times (Se_1 - Se_0)^2}

    For specificity:

    NSp=(z1−αSp0(1−Sp0)+z1−βSpSp1(1−Sp1))2(1−π)×(Sp1−Sp0)2 N_{Sp} = \frac{\left( z_{1-\alpha} \sqrt{Sp_0(1-Sp_0)} + z_{1-\beta_{Sp}} \sqrt{Sp_1(1-Sp_1)} \right)^2} {(1-\pi) \times (Sp_1 - Sp_0)^2}

    where:

    • z1−αz_{1-\alpha} is the one-sided critical value
    • z1−βz_{1-\beta} corresponds to the endpoint-specific power
    • Se0,Sp0Se_0, Sp_0 are null values
    • Se1,Sp1Se_1, Sp_1 are alternative values
    • π\pi is the prevalence; determines the allocation of diseased and non-diseased subjects.

    Root-Finding Condition

    The study must satisfy two conditions simultaneously:

    1. The overall power constraint

    (1−βSe)×(1−βSp)=(1−βOverall) (1-\beta_{Se}) \times (1-\beta_{Sp})=(1-\beta_{Overall})

    1. Equal total sample size requirement NSe=NSp N_{Se} = N_{Sp}

    Since the two endpoint-specific powers are linked through the overall power constraint, only one free parameter remains (e.g.,βSe\beta_{Se}).

    βSe=1−1−βOverall1−βSp \beta_{Se} = 1- \frac{1-\beta_{Overall}}{1-\beta_{Sp}}

    The algorithm therefore:

    • Express βSp\beta_{Sp} as a function of βSe\beta_{Se}
    • Substitutes into the two sample size formulas
    • Numerically solves for the value of βSe\beta_{Se} such that

    NSe(βSe)=NSp(βSp) N_{Se}(\beta_{Se}) = N_{Sp}(\beta_{Sp})

    This ensures that:

    • Both endpoints require the same total sample size
    • The overall power equals the desired target
    • The study is optimally balanced

    The resulting total sample size is Ntotal=NSe+NSpN_{total} = N_{Se} + N_{Sp} with allocation driven by prevalence.

    power_opt_bin()

    Computes the achieved overall power for a fixed total sample size and true prevalence π\pi in a confirmatory diagnostic accuracy study with co-primary endpoints.

    Endpoint - Specific Power Formula

    Given total NN and true prevalence π\pi:

    NSe=Ntotal⋅πandNSp=Ntotal⋅(1−π) N_{Se} = N_{total} \cdot \pi \quad\text{and}\quad N_{Sp} = N_{total} \cdot (1 - \pi)

    For sensitivity:

    zβSe=NSe|Se1−Se0|−z1−αSe0(1−Se0)Se1(1−Se1) z_{\beta_{Se}} = \frac{\sqrt{N_{Se}}|Se_1 - Se_0| - z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{Se_0(1-Se_0)}}{\sqrt{Se_1(1-Se_1)}}

    PowerSe=Φ(zβSe) Power_{Se} = \Phi(z_{\beta_{Se}})

    Similar for Specificity:

    zβSp=NSp|Sp1−Sp0|−z1−αSp0(1−Sp0)Sp1(1−Sp1) z_{\beta_{Sp}} = \frac{\sqrt{N_{Sp}}|Sp_1 - Sp_0| - z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{Sp_0(1-Sp_0)}}{\sqrt{Sp_1(1-Sp_1)}}

    PowerSp=Φ(zβSp) Power_{Sp} = \Phi(z_{\beta_{Sp}})

    The resulting overall power is

    Poweroverall=PowerSe×PowerSp Power_{overall} = Power_{Se} \times Power_{Sp}

    Remark
    Both functions rely on the same asymptotic normal approximation framework, ensuring mathematical consistency between sample size determination and power evaluation.

    Example

    Required Sample Size 

    
res <- ss_opt_bin(
  se1 = 0.85, sp1 = 0.85,
  se0 = 0.70, sp0 = 0.65,
  alpha = 0.025,
  prev = 0.5,
  pwr = 0.80
)

res
#> $pwr_se
#> [1] 0.820557
#> 
#> $pwr_sp
#> [1] 0.9749476
#> 
#> $N_se
#> [1] 66.77915
#> 
#> $N_sp
#> [1] 66.77915
#> 
#> $N_tot
#> [1] 133.5583

    Achieved Power for Fixed Sample Size 

    
pow<-power_opt_bin(
  N = res$N_tot,
  se1 = 0.85,sp1 = 0.85, 
  se0 = 0.70,sp0 = 0.65,
  alpha = 0.025,
  prev = 0.5
)
pow
#> $overall
#> [1] 0.8
#> 
#> $pwr_se
#> [1] 0.820557
#> 
#> $pwr_sp
#> [1] 0.9749476
